newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST -- U.S. Oct PPI may rise on energy prices.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST -- U.S. Oct PPI may rise on energy prices.

text.p: U.S. wholesale inflation may bounce mildly in October as a recent run-up in energy prices will likely put upward pressure on the overall Producer Price Index (PPI) to be released on Wednesday, analysts said.
"We're watching for the potential of higher energy prices to show up in the report," said Gary Thayer, senior economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc.
The jump in energy prices in October was largely seasonal. But pundits expressed concern about widespread price increases in oil-related items.
"Heating oil prices going up in October is not unusual, but we did have some gasoline price increases in October, which is a bit unusual," Thayer said.

But economists said a price drop in some sectors could offset the rise in energy prices. Pundits highlighted a drop in food prices, most notably in grains, as a key factor that may balance the rise in oil-related items.
"Our work sees energy and food offseting and I also think that ... those two sectors tend to get downplayed in the markets," said Alan Levenson, economist at UBS Securities.

In a Reuters survey, U.S. economists expect, on average, overall PPI to rise 0.2 percent in October. The core rate, which excludes food and energy price fluctuations, is seen up a tame 0.1 percent in October.
The report will be released at 0830 EST/1330 GMT on Wednesday.
"If you don't see (a sizable increase) in the core index, the markets will not react to it too meaningfully," Levenson said.
Some analysts also pointed to the possibility of slower increases in car prices as a positive factor keeping wholesale inflation under control.
"There's some downside risk that could come from seasonal adjustments of car prices," said Russell Sheldon, vice president and senior economist at Mellon Bank Corp.
Sheldon said he believes car price increases might be limited in the new model year due to tougher foreign competition, notably from Japanese automakers.
Analysts also said finished goods price gauges were expected to stay mostly stable.
"We expect to see good behavior on a year-to-year basis for the finished goods index," UBS's Levenson said.
If the report comes in as expected, analysts said the PPI data will mostly reiterate the market's belief that inflation remains under control for now.
That scenario, if confirmed, suggests the Federal Reserve might keep monetary policy on hold for the rest of the year, analysts said.
The Fed's current target for the federal funds rate is 5-1/4 percent. The target was last changed in January 1996, when the Fed trimmed the rate by 25 basis points.
"If the numbers come in as we've seen in the past couple of months it shows that things are doing well, inflation is tame and the Fed won't do anything," A.G. Edwards's Thayer said.
Most analysts see the Fed keeping rates unchanged at the next meeting of policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee on November 13.
